newsitem.title: UK: Sugar-Russia whites demand could tighten EU supply.
newsitem.headline: Sugar-Russia whites demand could tighten EU supply.

text.p: Russian demand for white sugar should further tighten EU supply while Cuban and Brazilian raws imports are refined but it will not dent availability into the summer, brokers said on Thursday.

Congestion at Novorossiisk and problems related to the financing of tolling operations were both cited as reasons to turn to shipping whites into Russia, as well as the chance of a profit from high internal prices.

"It takes a lot of time to get raws in, there's the financing and then the sugar sits in Novorossiisk," said one trader. "You can't ship raws from Cuba and have them ready in the market for the next week."
"It takes three days to get the whites in...it's a question of timing and finance," he said.
European producers have to reckon with 10 percent value-added tax on their exports into Russia, plus a hefty 25 percent import duty.

Traders said as many as five cargoes of white sugar might have entered Novorossiisk in recent weeks, while there was talk of 20,000 tonnes going into St Petersburg. But information was sketchy and unconfirmed, they added.
"There are parcels going in...and it's closing the gap for a short period of time," said another trader.
But he said the offtake was unlikely to restrict summer supply as there were still plenty of EU sugars which had yet to be licensed for export.
"I think it's just a short-term rush to make some money locally," he said.
One broker said while it made little sense to ship white sugar into Russia, some trade houses might be prepared to do so because tolling raws took so long.
"Anyone who does (ship whites) is just hoping for the prices to improve without wanting to wait for the time of getting raws tolled and in," he said.
"There isn't going to be a great flood of whites going in...there's always somebody who's going to take something in, but it's mainly raws."
Market sources said a handful of major trade houses were believed to be retaining one or two EU cargoes, possibly to create an artificial tightness and so boost prices for the summer.
"It's not that easy to buy a cargo. It is there but it's very tightly held in firm hands...and they're not letting it onto the market," said one.
"With the slight squeeze and the difficulty of getting cargoes, people don't want to sell short, and it comes back to the old adage -- don't be short at this time of the year," he said.

Details of raws shipments into Russia have been easier to track, with the constant trickle of Cuban arrivals and the expected large Brazilian delivery from U.S. trade house Cargill reflected in the freight market.
Not surprisingly, the large volumes of sugar have caused congestion and a backlog at Novorossisk, making it difficult for vessels to discharge their cargoes.
Earlier this week, some 90,000 tonnes of raws, mostly if not all of Cuban origin, was held up at the port. Port official said they expected this would take around one month to clear.
The backlog, down from 140,000 tonnes just under a month ago, has been blamed on bad weather and the lack of railway wagons to take sugar to refiners.
Traders played down the impact of the whites shipments, saying the emphasis was much more on raws. But the demand from Russia and other former Soviet Union nations had helped to underpin EU premiums.
Uzbekistan, for example, was thought to have been in the market last week to buy white sugar, traders said.

For prompt shipment, EU premiums are currently valued at $4 or slightly higher over London nearby futures and $4/6 bid/offer for August/September although traders said bids and offers for August EU sugars were scarce.
